title: Two loves: the poem and its 1599 printing
short: The speaker's two loves, the fair young man and the dark woman, set out as good and evil spirits; first printed in 1599.
body: This sonnet appeared, with Sonnet 138, in William Jaggard's miscellany The Passionate Pilgrim (1599), ten years before Thorpe's Quarto of the Sonnets; the archive also holds that earlier version separately. It is often taken as a summary of the triangle underlying the sequence: the young man of Sonnets 1-126 and the 'dark lady' of 127-152. 'Comfort and despair' are the two spiritual states between which a soul hovers: assurance of salvation, and the sin of despair. The poem treats a love triangle as a drama of salvation and damnation.

title: suggest me still
short: Tempt me constantly; 'suggest' had the strong sense of prompting to evil.
body: In Elizabethan English 'suggest' often meant to tempt or incite, especially of the devil (compare 'suggestion' in Macbeth 1.3 for the temptation to murder). 'Still' means always, continually. The two 'spirits' act on him like the good and bad angels who, in Christian tradition, attend each person and urge them towards virtue or sin. The verb is transitive here ('suggest me', tempt me), a construction now lost, which is why modern readers can miss how strong the word is.

title: better angel / worser spirit
short: The good and bad angels of the morality tradition, best known from Marlowe's Doctor Faustus.
body: The idea that each soul has a good and an evil angel competing for it is old, and allegories of the soul's battle go back to Prudentius's Psychomachia. On the Elizabethan stage it appears memorably in Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, where the Good and Evil Angels counsel Faustus in turn. Shakespeare maps it onto his two loves: the man is the better angel, the woman the worse. Many modern critics note how the poem's misogyny rests on these inherited schemes; others read the hierarchy as already ironised by the bawdy close.

title: colour'd ill
short: Of bad colouring: dark-complexioned, and also of evil character.
body: 'Colour'd ill' joins the physical and moral senses, as the Dark Lady sonnets do repeatedly (compare Sonnet 127, 'In the old age black was not counted fair', and Sonnet 147, 'as black as hell, as dark as night'). 'Right fair' (l. 3) is similarly double: fair-skinned and good. Critics have examined how this vocabulary ties darkness to evil, and scholars of early modern race, such as Kim F. Hall, have studied how such language shaped Renaissance ideas of colour.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale University Press, 1977), commentary on Sonnet 144

title: my female evil
short: The woman, his evil angel; 'evil' is compressed to one syllable to rhyme with 'devil'.
body: The phrase identifies the woman with evil itself, a misogynist commonplace rooted in readings of Eve in Genesis 3. 'Evil' was often pronounced as roughly one syllable, and it rhymes here with 'devil' (l. 7), both words probably sounded short. 'To win me soon to hell' states her aim: to bring him quickly to damnation by luring away his good angel.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale University Press, 1977), commentary on Sonnet 144

title: corrupt my saint to be a devil
short: To pervert the young man, his 'saint', into a devil: a temptation story told in theological terms.
body: Calling the young man a 'saint' extends the religious idiom of the poem. The change of an angel into a devil recalls the fall of Lucifer, and reverses Paul's warning that 'Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light' (2 Corinthians 11:14). 'Wooing his purity with her foul pride' sets fair purity against foul pride; 'pride' could also mean sexual desire or heat, a sense editors including Booth bring out here.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, 2 Corinthians 11:14

title: foul pride / fair pride: the 1599 and 1609 texts
short: The 1599 Passionate Pilgrim text differs from the 1609 Quarto in several places, most strikingly 'fair pride' for 'foul pride'.
body: The version in The Passionate Pilgrim (1599), also in the archive, reads 'That like two spirits', 'My better angel', 'her fair pride', 'For being both to me' and 'The truth I shall not know', where the 1609 text has 'Which like', 'The better angel', 'her foul pride', 'But being both from me' and 'Yet this shall I ne'er know'. Scholars debate whether the 1599 text preserves an earlier draft by Shakespeare, later revised, or is simply a corrupt copy that circulated in manuscript. 'Fair pride' gives an oxymoron of seductive beauty; 'foul pride' sharpens the moral contrast with 'purity'. The variants are an important piece of evidence that some sonnets circulated before 1609, as Francis Meres's 1598 mention of Shakespeare's 'sugared sonnets among his private friends' also suggests.

title: Suspect I may, yet not directly tell
short: I may suspect, but cannot say for certain: the speaker does not know whether the two are lovers.
body: 'Directly' means plainly, for certain. The third quatrain shifts from accusation to uncertainty: he suspects that his angel has turned fiend but lacks proof. Line 11, 'But being both from me, both to each friend', means 'since both are away from me and friends to each other', with 'friend' perhaps in the sense of lover. The poem is as much about jealous not-knowing as about sin, and the uncertainty is not resolved.

title: in another's hell
short: I guess one angel is in the other's hell: a bawdy double meaning, 'hell' as the woman's body.
body: On the surface the line means that the good angel is now in the bad angel's power, in her hell. But 'hell' was slang for the female genitals (as in Boccaccio's tale of putting the devil back in hell, Decameron 3.10), and editors including Booth and Duncan-Jones accept the sexual sense: the speaker suspects the young man is sleeping with the woman. Religious allegory and sexual pun run side by side, which is typical of the Dark Lady poems.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Yale University Press, 1977), commentary on Sonnet 144
Katherine Duncan-Jones, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (Arden Shakespeare, 3rd series, 1997; rev. 2010), note on Sonnet 144
Giovanni Boccaccio, Decameron, Day 3, Story 10

title: fire my good one out
short: Until the bad angel drives the good one out, as a fox is smoked from its hole, or infects him with venereal disease.
body: To 'fire out' was to drive out with fire, as foxes were smoked from their earths. Editors also hear a sexual and medical sense: he will know the truth only when the woman 'fires' the young man with venereal infection, the burning of the pox, or when she tires of him and expels him. The couplet ends in grim, bawdy uncertainty rather than resolution: 'live in doubt' looks back to the 'despair' of line 1. Compare the feverish close of Sonnet 147.
